name: create-and-remove-duplicate-runnable-events
description: A `whole_value` list is a MULTISET, and the protocol counts occurrences. `Runnable.events` imposes no uniqueness rule, so the same timing event may legitimately be recorded twice; clearing it takes one `remove` per occurrence, a `create` adds one occurrence, and the duplicate is never reported as `identity-conflict` — neither in the baseline nor in the staged result. Without this rule a duplicate would look like an identity collision, because in a `whole_value` collection the member's value IS its identity.

context.summary: The `examples/basic` model with two hand-edits to `ExampleSWC.ExampleRun`, whose declared `events` hold a single 10 ms trigger: that event is recorded TWICE (a copy-paste the model does not forbid), and a 20 ms timing event stands beside it. Both edits are legal — `schema.py` declares `events: list[TimingEvent | InitEvent]` with no uniqueness rule, `check-model` has none either, and `differ.py` keys the collection by value (`_value_key`). So the baseline holds three events: 0.01, 0.01 and 0.02. `ExampleRun` is mapped to no task, so retiming it binds no task-period rule; `Task_10ms` maps `ExampleConsumerSWC.ExampleConsumerRun`, not this runnable.

authorization.notes: One scope entry covers both removals: coverage is stated over an address, and in a multiset the two occurrences share one. The approval prompt therefore has to say how many occurrences go — which is what the delta below carries, one entry per occurrence.

input.intent: Retire both recorded occurrences of ExampleRun's 10 ms trigger, and record a second occurrence of the 20 ms trigger it already carries.

expected.notes: Three multiset rules in one exchange. (1) The duplicate in the baseline is LEGAL: `existing_elements` names the member address once because an address cannot say `twice`, and the summary says how many occurrences stand behind it — nothing here is an `identity-conflict`, because in a `whole_value` collection the member IS its identity and the collection counts rather than keys. (2) `remove` removes ONE occurrence, which is why the change set carries two of them; a single `remove` would have been accepted too and would have left one 10 ms trigger behind, with one delta entry instead of two. (3) `create` adds ONE occurrence, at the end of the list — and the created value is one the baseline ALREADY holds, which is the half of the rule a repeated `remove` cannot demonstrate. `existing_elements` names that member address, the `create` still succeeds, and `ExampleRun` ends with the 20 ms trigger recorded twice. At a uniquely identified address this would be an `identity-conflict`; in a multiset it is one more occurrence, so the delta carries one `create` rather than a collision. The delta counts the same way the collection does: one entry per occurrence added or removed, each at the member's own address, so two entries share an address and are not a repetition. What this vector is deliberately NOT: the same-identity replacement the protocol bans. A `remove` and a `create` of the same value in a multiset are one occurrence out and one occurrence in, and the ban's subject is uniquely identified elements and members — see `negative/identity-conflict-same-identity-group-move.json`. A `whole_value` MAP is the other side of that line: `SWComponent.memory`'s key is unique by construction, so a `create` at a key the baseline holds IS an `identity-conflict`.
